title: WHAT IF YOU FLEW 10 BILLION KM TO MERCURY?

segments.line: Eight years. Ten billion kilometres. Now four thrusters fire.
Miss this burn, and Mercury just flies past.
ESA's plan: capture into orbit on twenty-first November.
So what if you rode that spacecraft?
Welcome to Ifmosphere. Here are the rules.
You ride a stack: a European orbiter with a Japanese one tucked inside.
You ride a stack: a European orbiter with a Japanese one tucked inside.
At launch the whole stack weighed four thousand one hundred kilograms.
Fourteen hundred of those kilograms were just fuel.
Rule one. You can't steer live.
Earth is almost one hundred and fifty million kilometres away.
Every command takes eight point three minutes to arrive.
Confirmation takes the same again. That's sixteen minutes of silence.
Rule two. It's a one way trip.
And here's the catch. Mercury is a terrible place to arrive.
And here's the catch. Mercury is a terrible place to arrive.
Think a small planet near the Sun sounds easy? It's the opposite.
Fall toward the Sun, and the Sun speeds you up.
Faster, and faster, and faster.
To get captured, you have to throw that speed away.
ESA says it takes more energy than flying to Pluto.
Pluto. The planet-sized snowball at the edge of everything.
So the stack doesn't brake once. It cheats, nine times.
Flyby one is Earth, in April twenty twenty.
Then Venus. Twice. October twenty twenty, and August twenty twenty-one.
Then Venus. Twice. October twenty twenty, and August twenty twenty-one.
Then Mercury itself. Six flybys, each one a gravity brake.
Nine slingshots. A grand total of nine point nine billion kilometres.
Nine slingshots. A grand total of nine point nine billion kilometres.
That's about sixty-six times the distance from Earth to the Sun.
Remember the rule. No steering live.
Which means the brake burn is a script you wrote years ago.
But first, meet the planet you're aiming at.
Mercury is the smallest planet in the solar system.
But it's still half as big again as the Moon.
And four times heavier. That is a lot of planet for its size.
The reason hides inside. An unusually huge metal core.
Why so dense? That's one of the questions BepiColombo came to answer.
Why so dense? That's one of the questions BepiColombo came to answer.
Now the neighbourhood. Mercury sits thirty-six million miles from the Sun.
Now the neighbourhood. Mercury sits thirty-six million miles from the Sun.
That is just over a third of Earth's distance.
One Mercury day lasts fifty-eight Earth days of spinning.
The sun stays up three months. Then it stays down three months.
In the day the ground reaches four hundred and fifty degrees.
At night it drops to minus one hundred and eighty.
Hot enough to melt lead, cold enough to freeze air. Same rock.
Yet in the dark craters at the poles, there's ice.
Permanently shadowed. The sunlight never reaches the floor.
So that's your target. Now, what almost went wrong.
Your arrival was meant to be the fifth of December, twenty twenty-five.
Then, in April twenty twenty-four, a power fault.
Unexpected electrical currents, between a solar wing and a power unit.
The ion thrusters lost power. Your engines, running on a diet.
Mission control had one choice. Redo the entire route.
Arrival slipped by almost a whole year, to November twenty twenty-six.
Arrival slipped by almost a whole year, to November twenty twenty-six.
On fifteenth June twenty twenty-six, the ion drive switched off for good.
On third September, the transfer module let go.
About two hundred million kilometres from Earth.
That module had no antenna, no computer. Just a drifting box.
From here on, only the orbiter's chemical thrusters steer you.
So. The burn.
You come in over the south pole, on the night side.
Below you, nothing but black rock and a thin line of dawn.
Four of your thrusters fire together.
They push against your speed, every second, for a long burn.
Too short, and you skim away. Too long, and you dive in.
And you cannot touch the controls. Remember the sixteen minutes.
All you can do is watch the dot on the screen.
Then your speed slips below the planet's grip.
Mercury's gravity catches you. You're in orbit.
A wide, lopsided loop: five ninety by eleven thousand six hundred forty kilometres.
A wide, lopsided loop: five ninety by eleven thousand six hundred forty kilometres.
Low point, five ninety. High point, so far you almost leave.
Low point, five ninety. High point, so far you almost leave.
Mission control only learns it worked sixteen minutes later.
And remember, this is only one step of many.
ESA calls it a six-month arrival sequence.
Capture is the middle. The best parts come next.
On the ninth and tenth of December, the stack comes apart.
The European orbiter, MPO, lets go of the Japanese one, Mio.
On sixteenth December, Mio's sunshield drops away.
Then the two of you go your separate ways.
MPO drops low: four hundred and eighty by fifteen hundred kilometres.
It circles Mercury every two point three hours.
Mio swings wide: five ninety by eleven thousand six hundred forty.
Mio swings wide: five ninety by eleven thousand six hundred forty.
One lap takes nine point three hours. Long enough for a whole movie.
MPO keeps burning, to settle into its final orbit by March.
Science starts in April twenty twenty-seven.
Two spacecraft at one planet. That has never happened at Mercury.
Before you, only one spacecraft ever orbited Mercury. NASA's MESSENGER.
Before you, only one spacecraft ever orbited Mercury. NASA's MESSENGER.
That makes you second ever. Count Mariner Ten, and you're the third visit.
That makes you second ever. Count Mariner Ten, and you're the third visit.
So what does all that work buy you?
MPO carries eleven instruments. Mio carries five.
A laser will map the shape of the entire planet.
Cameras across many colours will read the surface rock.
And an X-ray eye will taste what the ground is made of.
It already passed its first test. Staring at the Crab Nebula.
Thirty-nine hours of looking, in September.
Fifty-five times the spacecraft turned, to nudge the view.
The picture came out slightly sharper than the lab test in twenty fifteen.
Eighty percent of that instrument's technology was brand new.
After eight years in space, its detector shows no radiation damage.
Mio will watch the magnetic field, and the solar wind hitting it.
It will taste the thin sodium haze that trails behind the planet.
Two spacecraft at once means one watches the wind arrive.
While the other measures what it does up close.
One orbiter alone could never do that. Remember the ice?
Scientists hope those spacecraft can finally say what the ice is.
Scientists hope those spacecraft can finally say what the ice is.
Here's the part nobody warns you about. You're not coming home.
The spacecraft are expected to orbit for about three years.
Then the fuel runs out, they lose height, and they land hard.
Their lead scientist put it simply. Sadly, they are not coming back.
It's a one point six billion euro goodbye, and it's worth every cent.
And you can wave at Mercury yourself, on a clear morning.
On twenty-first November it sits nineteen point six degrees from the Sun.
That's as far from the Sun as it ever gets this time round.
Brighter than almost every star. Find it low in the east.
Remember the cold open. Four thrusters. One burn. Ten billion kilometres.
Remember the cold open. Four thrusters. One burn. Ten billion kilometres.
Now you know why every second of it was a gamble.
Which planet would you try to orbit first?
Tomorrow: another What If.
Eight years to arrive. One planet to learn.
